The core insight is that habit formation is governed by reinforcement increments, which can be quantified as a function of temporal and contextual factors. Stimulus generalization emerges as a dual mechanism: it amplifies habit strength when stimuli are similar, yet attenuates it with increasing deviation. This leads to a mathematical formulation where sHR depends linearly on sH and exponentially on the deviation d. The adaptive significance lies in enabling flexible behavior under environmental variability. In GSE, this manifests as a dynamic state transition model where stimulus similarity drives behavioral modulation. In GSI, it becomes a Bayesian prior over stimulus-response mappings. The failure mode occurs when deviation exceeds discriminability thresholds, causing collapse of habit strength. This framework supports both predictive modeling and retroactive inference of behavioral patterns.
